name: spaghetti-code
intent: Records what Spaghetti Code costs: a control flow that no reader can trace — execution jumps where the syntax does not say it will, structures are tangled into one another, and the cost is that nobody can safely change a line because nobody can say what reaches it.
problem: Control flow is expressed with constructs that do not nest or compose — labels and `goto`, unstructured branches, ad-hoc flag variables carrying state between distant blocks, exception types invented as breaks — so the control graph of the program has edges the source text does not show. The behaviour is usually correct; the ability to reason about it is gone.
context: Historically the term names the `goto` tangle: control flow that jumps instead of nesting, whose logic cannot be followed without simulating the whole program, and whose sibling form uses exceptions or other unstructured branching constructs. Modern code produces it without `goto` at all, and the contemporary definitions are broader: convoluted control flow, no separation of responsibilities, excessive and unexpected dependencies, lack of modularity, reliance on global state instead of parameters, duplicated logic, inconsistent style, and insufficient documentation. The genuinely dangerous variant is not the `goto` but the OO-level tangle — one described in practitioner discussion as 'try to use every design pattern in the book even when they don't make sense', which produces spaghetti at the level of concept and is far more damaging than the lexical form, because it removes the model's explanatory power rather than just the reader's ability to follow jumps.
benefits: It is a diagnosis, not a style preference: naming the tangle converts 'this code is awful' into a concrete, orderable list of structural defects.

It has a measurable proxy. Cyclomatic complexity, maximum nesting depth, and the count of nonlocal jumps per function are all computable, so a refactoring can be justified with numbers rather than taste.

It identifies the first real remedy. Every listed symptom has a named structural fix — guard clauses for flag-driven branching, an explicit state machine for ad-hoc flags, Extract Method for a tangle of blocks.
It separates correctness from maintainability: a function can be correct and still be a smell, and calling it spaghetti says which of the two you are complaining about.
tradeoffs: Structured rewrites of tangle are high-risk without a safety net. Every transformation from flags to a state machine changes the reachable state space, and the combinations the original code never exercised are exactly the ones the tests do not cover.
Decomposing a tangle frequently exposes the real problem, which is a missing abstraction or a missing boundary — so the fix is larger than it looked and needs more than a cleanup pass.

Some apparent tangle is inherent. Interactive loops, parsers, protocol decoders and UI event handling legitimately have irregular control flow; forcing it into nested `if`s can make it worse and is why `while`/`switch`/`do-while` and state machines exist as alternatives to `goto`.

Legacy `goto` is sometimes load-bearing for cleanup in C (jumping out of nested initialisation or to a shared error path), where a single exit label is more readable than duplicated cleanup. The rule to apply is 'no backward jumps and no jumps into a block', not 'no goto'.
De-tangling code nobody understands is expensive and the estimate is always wrong; the honest approach is to add characterisation tests first and refactor under them, not to rewrite.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Discoverability is the lowest axis because the defining property is that no reader can determine which paths reach a given line without simulating execution — tooling that would otherwise make a change safe (coverage, call graphs, refactoring support) all become unreliable when the control graph does not match the text. Reliability is mid-low rather than minimal because tangled code frequently still works; the cost shows up as the rate of undetected change-induced defects, not as a crash rate.

participants.responsibility: The tangled body itself: mutually entangled control structures whose edges the source text does not express, so the control graph is not derivable by reading.
participants.notes: The Jargon File calls this structure "code with a complex and tangled control structure, esp. one using many GOTOs, exceptions, or other unstructured branching constructs".

participants.responsibility: The jump, label, exception or shared flag that connects two blocks that are not lexically nested, and is the reason the control graph exceeds the text.
participants.notes: Counting these per function is the cheapest detector available.

participants.responsibility: Anyone who must modify the code, including its author six months later, and who must simulate the program to know which paths reach a change.
participants.notes: Nobody can review a change safely here, which is why the smell is a delivery risk rather than an aesthetic complaint.

use_cases: A BASIC or COBOL routine where `GOTO` handles both looping and error exits, so the control graph must be simulated to see whether a loop can re-enter incorrectly.
Procedural code written into classes: methods hundreds of lines long, with `self`-scoped flag attributes (`self._found = False`) standing in for control state.
Exception types used as breaks — a custom `BreakOutOfLoop` raised and caught two frames up — to escape deeply nested loops that a labelled break could have handled.
Deeply nested `if`/`else` chains (five or more levels) where the innermost branch is unreachable in practice and nobody can tell without checking.
A system where every module imports every other module and the dependency graph is a single blob, so control never travels in a readable direction.

Applying the catalogue wholesale: a class that mixes Strategy, Observer, Decorator and a state machine for a problem that needed none of them, so the intent can no longer be inferred from the structure.
avoid_when: Interactive loops, state machines, protocol decoders and event handlers, where irregular control flow is the domain. Write them as explicit state machines with a switch, not as nested conditionals.
A single forward `goto` used as an early exit in C, where a flag variable or duplicated cleanup would be worse; the rule that matters is no backward jumps and no jumps into a block.
Generated code, lexer/parser output and machine-translated sources — never maintain it by hand, regenerate it instead.
Assembly, coroutine trampolines and deliberately obfuscated or packed code, where the tangle is the specification.
Code that is about to be deleted: the cheapest de-tangling of all is removing it.
pitfalls: Calling untidy code spaghetti and then only running a formatter, which changes the text without changing the control graph.
Rewriting a tangle from scratch. The behaviour encoded in the tangle is often the only specification of what the program actually does, including the bugs callers depend on.
Splitting a long function into short ones without changing the control flow, which produces many short functions nobody can still reason about.
Converting flag-based branching into a state machine and thereby *increasing* the reachable state space beyond what the tests cover.
Treating the absence of `goto` as proof of absence: modern spaghetti is produced by dependency cycles, exception-as-control-flow and wholesale pattern use.

related_patterns_notes.state: State is the structured answer to the most common form of spaghetti in OO code: ad-hoc boolean flags replaced by one enumeration whose transitions are declared, so the reachable state space is inspectable.
related_patterns_notes.guard-clause: Guard clauses invert the deep `if` nesting that flag-driven spaghetti produces, putting the happy path last at the shallowest depth.
related_patterns_notes.trampoline: A trampoline replaces mutual recursion and deep call chains with an explicit work list, which is the structured version of a control graph built from nonlocal returns.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Chain of Responsibility distributes a decision across a chain of handlers instead of concentrating it in nested conditionals; it is a structure to reach for when a tangle is a growing decision tree, not a single tangled block.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy is the answer when the tangle is a growing family of parallel conditionals over a kind; the anti-pattern of applying Strategy to a problem with one variant is itself a form of concept-level spaghetti.

anti_patterns: The forward-and-backward `goto` web: labels above and below the intended block, with the loop condition implicit in the jump target rather than in a loop header.
Exception types invented as loop breaks or early returns, which are the modern equivalent of a nonlocal jump.
Self-scoped flag attributes standing in for control state (`self._valid`, `self._seen_first`, `self._retry`) that are read in distant methods, so the flag is invisible in the method that tests it.
Nested conditionals five or more deep with no early exit, so the error case lives at the bottom of the tree.
Nested loops with `break`/`continue` at several levels and no label, so the break's target must be counted.
A dependency graph that is a single blob: every module imports every other module, so control never travels in one readable direction.

Concept-level spaghetti: applying the whole pattern catalogue to a problem that needed two of them, which is described in practitioner discussion as far more damaging than lexical spaghetti because it destroys the model's explanatory power.
Global mutable state used in place of parameters, which produces the same unreadability as flag-driven control flow at whole-program scale.
design_principles: Go to considered harmful: structured control flow (sequence, selection, iteration) is preferred because its nesting is the program's structure; a jump is a statement that the structure does not explain.
Single entry, single exit per unit, with early exits expressed as guard clauses rather than jumps to a common tail.
Declare state, do not infer it: if control position is represented by variables, those variables should be an explicit enumeration whose transitions are the only way to change it.
Cohesion and small units: the deeper reason long functions are hard is that the semantic distance between what a method does and how it does it grows until the name stops describing the body.
Make the control graph derivable from the text: an edge in the control flow should be visible in the syntax, or the structure is not doing its job.
best_practices: Measure before rewriting: cyclomatic complexity, maximum nesting depth and the count of nonlocal exits per function are computable and give a refactoring an objective budget.
Write characterisation tests for the tangle before touching it — the tangle is the de facto specification, including its bugs, and the tests are what let you keep them.
Decompose in order: Extract Method on coherent blocks first, then replace flag-driven branching with an explicit state, then remove the flag attributes that no longer exist.
Replace nonlocal exits with the language's structured equivalent: labelled break/continue, a state machine switch, or early `return` with guard clauses.
Add a lint gate: complexity thresholds, nesting-depth limits and a rule banning backward `goto` catch regressions at review time rather than at inspection time.
Where a dependency cycle is the real tangle, fix the cycle — invert the dependency with an interface or an event — rather than reordering statements.
For OO 'spaghetti' (long methods, lost polymorphism, procedural style in classes), the named moves are Extract Class and Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, not shorter methods alone.
When the honest answer is a rewrite, rewrite behind the characterisation tests and a facade so the rest of the system does not notice.
sources: Dijkstra, 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' (1965) and the structured-programming literature it launched — the origin of the judgement that unstructured jumps are a defect rather than a style.
